title: Probing The Nature Of Radial Flow: Evidence of its collective origin in Pb+Pb collisions with the ATLAS detector

22nd International Conference on Strangeness in Quark Matter (SQM 2026) Los Angeles, California · March 24, 2026
Presented on behalf of the ATLAS Collaboration.

title: Probing The Nature Of Radial Flow: Evidence of its collective origin in Pb+Pb collisions with the ATLAS detector
text:
Summary
This presentation reports the first measurement of the transverse-momentum dependence of radial-flow fluctuations, \(v_0(p_T)\), over \(0.5 < p_T < 10\) GeV in Pb+Pb collisions at \(\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=5.02\) TeV with the ATLAS detector. The measurement satisfies three major hallmarks of collectivity: \(p_T\) factorization, long-range correlations in pseudorapidity, and a centrality-independent response shape. Comparisons with hydrodynamic models further demonstrate the sensitivity of \(v_0(p_T)\) to the bulk viscosity of the QGP.

title: Revealing the Bowling-Pin Geometry of Ne via O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions with ATLAS
text:
The 8th International Conference on the Initial Stages of High-Energy Nuclear Collisions (Initial Stages 2025) Taipei, Taiwan · September 11, 2025
Plenary Talk · Presented on behalf of the ATLAS Collaboration.

title: Revealing the Bowling-Pin Geometry of Ne via O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions with ATLAS
text:
Summary
This presentation reported the first ATLAS measurements of azimuthal flow in O+O and Ne+Ne collisions at a nucleon-pair center-of-mass energy of 5.36 TeV. By comparing two light nuclei of similar size but different predicted intrinsic shapes, the measurement uses collective flow as a probe of nuclear geometry.
In the most central collisions, Ne+Ne exhibits approximately 10% larger elliptic flow than O+O while the triangular flow of the two systems remains similar. Together with multi-particle cumulant measurements, these observations provide evidence for the elongated, bowling-pin-like geometry of the neon nucleus. The measured transverse-momentum dependence of the flow harmonics also displays behavior qualitatively similar to that seen in larger heavy-ion systems, supporting a collective origin for the observed anisotropy.

title: Nuclear Shape Fluctuations in Heavy-Ion Collisions

title: Nuclear Shape Fluctuations in Heavy-Ion Collisions
text:
Summary
Nuclear deformation influences the geometry of the initial state created in heavy-ion collisions. This presentation explored what happens when the nuclear shape itself is allowed to fluctuate from event to event, rather than being described by fixed deformation parameters.
Using analytical estimates and Glauber-model calculations, the study examined fluctuations of the quadrupole deformation magnitude and triaxiality and their impact on initial-state observables related to the shape and transverse size of the collision system. Particular attention was given to how these nuclear-shape fluctuations modify the moments and correlations of the eccentricity and inverse transverse size.
The results illustrate how high-energy heavy-ion collisions can provide sensitivity not only to the average deformation of a nucleus, but also to fluctuations around its equilibrium shape, providing a connection between nuclear-structure physics and experimentally accessible collective observables.

title: Probing Effect of Nuclear Shape Coexistence in Heavy-Ion Collisions using Glauber Model
text:
Summary
Nuclear geometry can exhibit fluctuations beyond a fixed average deformation, including shape coexistence between competing nuclear configurations. This poster investigated how such shape fluctuations influence the initial geometry of high-energy heavy-ion collisions.
Using a Glauber Monte Carlo model, the study examined the effect of nuclear shape coexistence on observables including eccentricity and transverse-area fluctuations. The results demonstrated that multiparticle correlations in heavy-ion collisions can retain sensitivity to fluctuations of the underlying nuclear shape.

title: Impact of Nuclear Shape Fluctuations in High-Energy Heavy-Ion Collisions
text:
Aman Dimri, Somadutta Bhatta, Jiangyong Jia
The European Physical Journal A 59, 45 (2023)

title: Impact of Nuclear Shape Fluctuations in High-Energy Heavy-Ion Collisions
text:
Overview
Nuclei are often described by a single average shape, such as spherical, prolate, or oblate. In reality, the nuclear wave function may contain a distribution of shapes: the magnitude of the deformation and its triaxiality can both fluctuate. High-energy heavy-ion collisions offer a complementary way to investigate these fluctuations. The initial positions of the participating nucleons determine the geometry of the matter created in the collision, which in turn influences the subsequent collective expansion.
This project asks how fluctuations of intrinsic nuclear shape affect the initial collision geometry, and whether the average deformation can be separated from its fluctuations. Using analytical estimates and Monte Carlo Glauber simulations, we study two initial-state observables: elliptic eccentricity, \(\varepsilon_2\), and the inverse transverse size, \(d_\perp\). They are related, respectively, to elliptic flow and event-by-event variations of mean transverse momentum. We find that fluctuations of deformation magnitude modify their variances and higher-order cumulants, while fluctuations of triaxiality progressively wash out the distinction between prolate and oblate shapes.

title: Impact of Nuclear Shape Fluctuations in High-Energy Heavy-Ion Collisions
text:
Analysis

Beyond a fixed nuclear shape
A quadrupole-deformed nucleus can be characterized by two parameters: \(\beta\), the magnitude of its deformation, and \(\gamma\), its triaxiality. In this convention, \(\gamma=0\) describes a prolate shape, \(\gamma=\pi/3\) an oblate shape, and \(\gamma=\pi/6\) a maximally triaxial shape. A conventional fixed-shape calculation assigns a constant pair \((\beta,\gamma)\) to each nucleus and averages only over its spatial orientation.
Here we additionally allow the nuclear shape itself to fluctuate. The model samples \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) from distributions characterized by their means \((\bar\beta,\bar\gamma)\) and widths \((\sigma_\beta,\sigma_\gamma)\). This separates two physically different questions: what is the average nuclear shape? and how broadly does the nucleus fluctuate around that shape? The collision observables need not respond to these two properties in the same way.






Figure 1: Schematic representation of nuclear-shape fluctuations. Different intrinsic configurations contribute to the event-by-event distribution of collision geometries. This is a conceptual illustration, not a Glauber-model result.





Connecting nuclear shape to the collision geometry
For each event, the positions of the participants define the complex elliptic eccentricity and an inverse-size measure,
\[
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_2
=-\frac{\langle r_\perp^2e^{2i\phi}\rangle_{\mathrm{part}}}
{\langle r_\perp^2\rangle_{\mathrm{part}}},
\qquad
d_\perp=\sqrt{\frac{N_{\mathrm{part}}}
{\langle r_\perp^2\rangle_{\mathrm{part}}}}.
\]
Here the averages are over participating nucleons in a single event. \(\varepsilon_2=|\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_2|\) measures the ellipticity of the initial transverse distribution, whereas \(d_\perp\) increases when the overlap region becomes more compact at comparable participant number. In a collective response picture, \(v_2\simeq\kappa_2\varepsilon_2\) and fluctuations of \(d_\perp\) are related to variations of radial expansion and \([p_T]\). These are connections to final-state observables; the calculations in this paper are performed at the initial-state level, rather than with full hydrodynamic evolution.


Modeling event-by-event deformation fluctuations
The study uses a deformed Woods-Saxon nucleon distribution and Monte Carlo Glauber simulations of ultra-central \(^{238}\)U+\(^{238}\)U collisions at zero impact parameter. This setting suppresses the geometric anisotropy associated with a nonzero impact parameter and makes the effects of intrinsic deformation easier to isolate. For each nucleus, the model samples its deformation parameters and a random orientation before computing participant positions and the corresponding \(\varepsilon_2\) and \(d_\perp\).
Analytical leading-order relations guide the interpretation, while extensive nucleon-Glauber calculations quantify higher-order corrections. A constituent-quark Glauber calculation provides a separate check of the qualitative trends. This combination lets us distinguish robust dependencies on the deformation moments from details of the initial-state model.


What do the higher-order observables reveal?
To leading order, the deformation-dependent part of the second moments of \(\varepsilon_2\) and \(d_\perp\) is governed by
\[
\langle\beta^2\rangle=\bar\beta^2+\sigma_\beta^2.
\]
Consequently, a two-particle observable alone cannot generally determine whether a larger fluctuation signal comes from a larger average deformation or from stronger event-by-event fluctuations of that deformation. Higher-order observables offer complementary sensitivity. Mixed three-particle correlations between eccentricity and inverse size, and the third moment of inverse-size fluctuations, depend at leading order on \(\langle\beta^3\cos(3\gamma)\rangle\). Four-particle eccentricity cumulants also probe \(\langle\beta^4\rangle\) and combinations of lower moments. The higher moments therefore carry information not contained in the variance alone.
In particular, a wider distribution in \(\beta\) modifies not only the variance but also the skewness and kurtosis of the initial-state observables. The numerical study demonstrates where leading-order expectations work and where higher-order contributions become important. These effects are presented in detail in the published paper.


Why triaxiality fluctuations matter
The response to \(\gamma\) fluctuations has a distinct pattern. For a Gaussian distribution of \(\gamma\),
\[
\langle\cos(3\gamma)\rangle
=e^{-9\sigma_\gamma^2/2}\cos(3\bar\gamma).
\]
Thus, increasing \(\sigma_\gamma\) suppresses the leading term that distinguishes prolate and oblate configurations in the three-particle observables. In the large-fluctuation limit of the model, their predictions converge toward those for a rigid triaxial nucleus. A nucleus whose triaxiality fluctuates widely may therefore look quite different from a nucleus with the same mean shape held fixed. This makes it essential to account for shape fluctuations when interpreting flow-based nuclear-structure constraints.


Can the mean deformation and its fluctuations be separated?
A central result of the paper is a strategy for constraining both \(\bar\beta\) and \(\sigma_\beta\). Since the second eccentricity moment primarily measures \(\langle\beta^2\rangle\), we examined a combination of the second and fourth moments,
\[
F_K=\langle\varepsilon_2^4\rangle
-K\langle\varepsilon_2^2\rangle^2,
\]
with \(K\) chosen to minimize sensitivity to \(\sigma_\beta\). In the nucleon-Glauber study, an optimized value near \(K=2.54\) produces a quantity that depends mainly on \(\bar\beta^4\). The mean deformation inferred in this way can then be combined with the second moment to constrain the fluctuation width.
This is a model-tested method, not a model-independent determination of nuclear deformation from experimental data. Its separation power becomes weaker when the fluctuations are comparable to or larger than the mean deformation, and quantitative application to measured flow requires control of the subsequent hydrodynamic response. Nevertheless, the construction illustrates why combining cumulants of different orders is more informative than relying on one observable.

title: Impact of Nuclear Shape Fluctuations in High-Energy Heavy-Ion Collisions
text:
My Contribution
As the first author, I investigated the effects of quadrupole-deformation and triaxiality fluctuations on collision geometry using Monte Carlo simulations. My work focused on the distributions and higher-order correlations of \(\varepsilon_2\) and \(d_\perp\), including how different moments respond to the mean nuclear shape and its event-by-event fluctuations. The study also developed and tested combinations of eccentricity moments that can help separate the average deformation from its fluctuation width.

title: Impact of Nuclear Shape Fluctuations in High-Energy Heavy-Ion Collisions
text:
Broader Implications
The work connects intrinsic nuclear-structure fluctuations with the collective observables of relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Because elliptic flow and mean transverse momentum respond to different aspects of the same initial geometry, their moments and correlations offer complementary constraints on nuclear shape. The central lesson is that extracting a nuclear deformation from high-energy collisions requires accounting for both its mean and its fluctuations.
This approach complements traditional nuclear-structure measurements and motivates combined studies of elliptic flow, radial-flow fluctuations, and higher-order cumulants across collision systems. Future comparisons with full hydrodynamic calculations and data can test how much of the initial-state sensitivity survives into experimentally measured observables. A complementary experimental example is the ATLAS O+O and Ne+Ne flow measurement, which tests the sensitivity of collective flow to the intrinsic shapes of light nuclei.

title: Particle Production in High Energy Collisions
text:
Overview
My Master’s thesis brought together two complementary parts of my training: reconstructing the mathematical foundations of statistical mechanics and applying statistical and dynamical models to high-energy nuclear collisions. I began by working through the theory of quantum gases, their thermodynamics, and systematic treatments of interactions. I then used that framework to study hadronic matter, particle production, and collective flow in relativistic heavy-ion collisions.
The initial chapters were primarily an exercise in understanding established physics at the level of derivations. Working principally from Kerson Huang’s Statistical Mechanics (Huang 1987), I developed my own calculations and explanations of the underlying results. These chapters document independent reconstructions of established derivations, building the analytical command I wanted before applying the theory. The later chapters applied the framework to the hadron resonance gas (HRG), chemical freeze-out, and comparisons of transport and hydrodynamic calculations with heavy-ion measurements.

title: Particle Production in High Energy Collisions
text:
Reconstructing Statistical Mechanics

From quantum statistics to thermodynamics
I developed the treatments of ideal Fermi and Bose gases starting from quantum-state counting and the grand canonical ensemble. The calculation connects the mean occupation of single-particle states,
n¯(E)=1exp⁡[β(E−μ)]±1,
\overline{n}(E)=\frac{1}{\exp[\beta(E-\mu)]\pm1},

with macroscopic observables such as pressure, particle density, internal energy, and specific heat. Here the plus sign describes fermions and the minus sign describes bosons. I considered non-relativistic and relativistic regimes, including zero- and finite-temperature limits.
The derivations extended to familiar but instructive examples: blackbody radiation, phonon thermodynamics, and Bose–Einstein condensation. Working through these results established how the same statistical-mechanical formalism describes apparently different physical systems.


Introducing interactions and approximation schemes
I next studied how the ideal-gas picture changes when particles have interactions or a finite excluded volume. This part developed classical and quantum cluster expansions, virial coefficients, low-temperature treatments of imperfect quantum gases, and the van der Waals approach to the equation of state.
A central lesson was the relationship between microscopic assumptions, approximation schemes, and observable thermodynamic quantities. These mathematical tools prepared the transition from idealized gases to a system containing many hadronic species. The treatment draws on Huang’s textbook and, for the nuclear-matter applications, research literature cited in the original thesis.

title: Particle Production in High Energy Collisions
section: Applying Statistical Mechanics to Hadronic Matter
text:
Applying Statistical Mechanics to Hadronic Matter

The hadron resonance gas
The HRG model describes a thermal system using the known hadron spectrum. I compared ideal HRG, excluded-volume HRG, and an interacting van der Waals formulation by calculating thermodynamic quantities and comparing them with lattice-QCD results at zero chemical potential.
The comparisons showed that the treatment of interactions—and whether mesons and baryons are modeled together or as distinct subsystems—substantially affects the predictions. In particular, treating the mesons as ideal while including van der Waals interactions in the baryonic sector improved agreement with the lattice-QCD curves for the model parameters and thermodynamic range considered in the thesis.






Figure 1: Thermodynamic comparisons from the interacting hadron resonance gas: normalized pressure, number density, energy density and entropy density, with model results and reference data. Original Figure 30 of my Master’s thesis.





Particle yields and chemical freeze-out
I then investigated particle production in Au+Au collisions using statistical and transport descriptions. With the THERMUS thermal-model package, I extracted chemical freeze-out parameters from measured hadron yields and compared the results with those reported by the STAR Collaboration.
I also studied particle-yield predictions from the AMPT transport model at sNN=7.7GeV\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=7.7\,\mathrm{GeV}, contrasting its default and string-melting configurations with the STAR measurements. The model described the pion and proton yields more successfully than the kaon yields in the scenarios examined. This comparison illustrated both the utility and the limits of the model description.






Figure 2: Particle-yield comparisons for pions, kaons and protons across collision centralities in AMPT default and string-melting scenarios, compared with STAR data. Original Figure 35 of my Master’s thesis.

title: Particle Production in High Energy Collisions
text:
Collective Flow and Hydrodynamic Evolution
The final research part explored whether collective-flow observables could distinguish the model scenarios used to represent predominantly hadronic and QGP-like evolution. I studied elliptic and triangular flow, v2v_2 and v3v_3, using AMPT calculations and compared elliptic-flow behavior with hydrodynamic simulations employing different equations of state.
One focus was number-of-constituent-quark (NCQ) scaling. In the studied AMPT configurations, the string-melting scenario showed approximate NCQ scaling of elliptic flow and a modified scaling behavior for triangular flow, while the default configuration showed weaker scaling. These are model-dependent results, supporting the interpretation that the partonic-stage dynamics affect the measured flow patterns rather than providing a universal, model-independent test of QGP formation.









Figure 3: NCQ-scaled elliptic flow in the default and string-melting AMPT configurations. Original Figure 45 of the thesis.











Figure 4: Modified NCQ scaling for triangular flow in the same two AMPT scenarios. Original Figure 47 of the thesis.






The comparison with hydrodynamic calculations provided a complementary perspective: the calculated elliptic flow depended on the assumed equation of state and on the evolution model, and the scenarios could be examined against STAR measurements.






Figure 5: Elliptic-flow comparison from AMPT and hydrodynamic model scenarios with STAR data. Original Figure 51 of the thesis.

title: Particle Production in High Energy Collisions
text:
What This Thesis Established
The thesis helped me develop a working command of statistical mechanics through detailed derivation, and then put that understanding to use in nuclear-physics calculations. It brought together analytical reasoning, numerical modeling, comparisons with experimental measurements, and the need to interpret results within the assumptions of each model. Those foundations have continued to shape my approach to research in relativistic heavy-ion physics.

The plots shown here are direct reproductions of figures from my 2021 Master’s thesis (Figs. 30, 35, 45, 47, and 51), cropped for readability without reconstructing or modifying their numerical content. Their original methods, data sources, and additional references are documented in the full thesis.

title: What Information Does Differential Radial Flow Carry?
text:
Somadutta Bhatta, Aman Dimri, Jiangyong Jia
Nuclear Science and Techniques 37, 163 (2026)

title: What Information Does Differential Radial Flow Carry?
text:
Overview
The differential radial-flow observable \(v_0(p_T)\) measures how fluctuations of the particle spectrum at a given transverse momentum correlate with event-by-event changes in the mean transverse momentum, \([p_T]\). Its momentum-dependent shape can provide information about collective radial expansion and the transport properties of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP). But the way a spectrum is normalized, or the way events are classified by activity, can also affect the numerical value of the observable.
This project addresses a central interpretational question: which features of \(v_0(p_T)\) reflect the underlying dynamics, and which depend on analysis conventions? Using analytical relations and HIJING simulations, we show that different spectral-normalization ranges and centrality estimators can produce a constant vertical offset in \(v_0(p_T)\) without changing its dependence on \(p_T\). The location where the curve crosses zero is therefore not an invariant measure of radial-flow dynamics. The robust information resides in its differential shape, or equivalently in its derivative with respect to \(p_T\).

title: What Information Does Differential Radial Flow Carry?
text:
Analysis

What does differential radial flow measure?
An event contains a transverse-momentum spectrum \(N(p_T)\), whose integral gives the total number of particles \(N\). We can separate its overall normalization from its momentum-dependent shape by writing
\[
N(p_T)=N\,n(p_T),\qquad \int n(p_T)\,dp_T=1.
\]
The normalized spectrum \(n(p_T)\) describes how the particle yield is distributed in transverse momentum, while \(N\) describes the global multiplicity. A change in radial expansion typically changes the shape of the spectrum: stronger radial flow produces a flatter distribution and a larger event-wise mean \([p_T]\). The observable \(v_0(p_T)\) quantifies the correlation of local spectral fluctuations with those of \([p_T]\).
The distinction between normalization and shape is essential. In real analyses, particles are measured over finite momentum intervals, and multiplicity still fluctuates among events selected within the same centrality bin. An observed change in \(v_0(p_T)\) need not therefore imply a change in the underlying radial-flow response.


How global multiplicity creates an offset
For small correlated fluctuations, the spectrum can be decomposed to leading order as
\[
\delta N(p_T)\simeq
\langle n(p_T)\rangle\,\delta N
+\langle N\rangle\,\delta n(p_T).
\]
The first term represents a global change in particle number, whereas the second captures a change in the normalized spectral shape. A differential observable constructed from the unnormalized spectrum \(N(p_T)\) therefore contains a multiplicity contribution in addition to the shape contribution measured from \(n(p_T)\).
The two definitions, denoted \(v_0'(p_T)\) and \(v_0(p_T)\), obey the approximate relation
\[
\Delta v_0\equiv v_0'(p_T)-v_0(p_T)
\simeq \rho(N,[p_T])\frac{\sigma_N}{\langle N\rangle},
\]
where \(\rho(N,[p_T])\) is the correlation coefficient between multiplicity and mean transverse momentum, and \(\sigma_N\) is the standard deviation of \(N\). Crucially, the right-hand side is independent of \(p_T\). Residual volume or centrality fluctuations thus displace the entire curve rather than changing its shape. The relation is derived under the small-correction approximations appropriate to narrow event-activity selections.


The ambiguity introduced by a finite normalization range
Normalizing the spectrum does not completely remove the ambiguity, because the normalization itself depends on the accepted momentum interval. Define \(N_R=\int_R N(p_T)\,dp_T\) and \(n_R(p_T)=N(p_T)/N_R\) for a chosen range \(R\). Even at fixed total multiplicity, \(N_R\) can fluctuate as particles enter or leave the selected interval. Changing \(R\) therefore changes the residual multiplicity contribution to \(v_0(p_T)\).






Figure 1: Schematic of the constant-offset result. Spectral normalization over 0-10, 0.5-10, or 1-10 GeV changes the vertical position and zero crossing of \(v_0(p_T)\) while preserving its differential shape. The drawing illustrates the interpretation; it is not a plot of HIJING output.



This explains why a zero crossing near the ensemble mean \(p_T\) is not a unique dynamical scale: changing the normalization interval can move the crossing even when the same underlying spectral fluctuations are being studied.


Testing the argument with HIJING
We tested these relations in Pb+Pb events generated with HIJING, which provides a useful non-collective baseline rather than a hydrodynamic description of radial flow. The study varied the event-activity estimator, the momentum range used to normalize the spectrum, and the reference momentum interval used to define \([p_T]\). The correlations were constructed using separated subevents to reduce short-range biases and to test the expected multiplicity-dependent contributions.
The results support the analytical picture. Changing the event-activity definition causes substantial shifts for the observable constructed from the unnormalized spectrum; using the normalized spectrum or subtracting the predicted global-multiplicity contribution largely removes those shifts. Changing the spectral-normalization interval also displaces the curves, and the calculated correction brings them into close agreement. The corresponding comparisons are shown in the article’s results figures.
The reference-\(p_T\) dependence of the HIJING results additionally reveals non-flow contributions, especially at high \(p_T\). These effects should not be confused with the constant baseline ambiguity: they can alter the momentum-dependent behavior itself. HIJING is therefore used here to separate methodological and non-flow effects, not as evidence for collective expansion.


Why the zero crossing is not the physical observable
The measured \(v_0(p_T)\) may be negative at low momentum and positive at higher momentum, with a zero crossing between the two. That crossing is visually convenient, but its location depends on the vertical baseline. Since changing analysis conventions can modify the baseline without modifying the physical spectral-shape response, the crossing point alone is not a reliable dynamical scale.
Instead, a common additive offset cancels from any difference between two momentum points,
\[
\bigl[v_0(p_{T,1})+C\bigr]-\bigl[v_0(p_{T,2})+C\bigr]
=v_0(p_{T,1})-v_0(p_{T,2}),
\]
and from the derivative
\[
v_{0s}(p_T)\equiv\frac{d v_0(p_T)}{dp_T}.
\]
These shape-sensitive quantities avoid the normalization ambiguity. The derivative is proposed as a useful alternative observable; the paper does not claim that the derivative has already been measured experimentally.


Implications for experimental comparisons
Different experiments use different detector acceptances, momentum cuts, spectrum-normalization conventions, and event-activity selections. Directly comparing the absolute positions or zero crossings of their \(v_0(p_T)\) curves can therefore be misleading. A meaningful comparison should first place the measurements on a common normalization convention or align their baselines, then compare their \(p_T\) dependence.
This distinction is especially important when using differential radial flow to constrain the QGP’s transport properties. A model that reproduces the slope and curvature but differs by an additive offset need not have an incorrect dynamical response. Conversely, agreement in the zero-crossing position alone does not establish agreement in the physical spectral-shape fluctuations.

title: What Information Does Differential Radial Flow Carry?
text:
My Contribution
I proposed the constant-offset interpretation of differential radial-flow curves obtained with different momentum ranges and analysis conventions. I also derived the analytical relations connecting global multiplicity fluctuations to the displacement of \(v_0(p_T)\), providing the basis for the paper’s interpretation and its HIJING-based validation. This work helped distinguish robust momentum-dependent physics from normalization-dependent features of the observable.

title: What Information Does Differential Radial Flow Carry?
section: Connection to the ATLAS Radial-Flow Measurement
text:
Connection to the ATLAS Radial-Flow Measurement
This study complements the ATLAS measurement that established long-range correlations, factorization, and a common differential response shape for radial flow in Pb+Pb collisions. The ATLAS work provides experimental evidence for collectivity; the present study explains how residual multiplicity fluctuations and normalization choices affect the interpretation of the differential observable. Together, they clarify what should be compared when using \(v_0(p_T)\) to study the collective medium.

title: What Information Does Differential Radial Flow Carry?
text:
Broader Implications
The broader lesson is that a differential observable can contain both dynamical information and an analysis-dependent baseline. Recognizing which features are invariant under changes of normalization makes comparisons between experiments and models more reliable. For radial flow, this focuses attention on the shape of \(v_0(p_T)\) as the part that can be used to study the medium’s response and, ultimately, constrain properties such as bulk viscosity.

Illustration: ATLAS Experiment © CERN, 2022 detector schematic. Focus markers are approximate educational annotations calibrated to this illustration.

Inner Tracking Detector
The first clues are the paths charged particles leave behind.
What it measures: Positions of charged particles moving through a magnetic field.
Why it matters: The curved tracks help reveal particle momenta and where the particles came from.


Electromagnetic Calorimeter
The barrel forms a cylindrical layer. The end-cap calorimeter assemblies also contain electromagnetic sections.
What it measures: Energy deposited by electromagnetic showers from electrons and photons.
Why it matters: Together with tracking information, the deposited energy helps identify electrons and photons. The end-cap assemblies also contain hadronic calorimetry.


Hadronic Calorimeter
Outside the electromagnetic calorimeter sits a much thicker layer built to measure hadronic showers.
What it measures: Energy deposited by hadrons, including protons, neutrons, and particles produced in jets.
Why it matters: Its measurements complement the electromagnetic calorimeter and help reconstruct jets and the total energy balance of a collision.


Solenoid Magnet
A thin superconducting coil encircles the inner tracking detector.
What it does: The solenoid produces a magnetic field that bends charged tracks; it does not directly detect particles.
Why it matters: The bending direction reveals electric charge, while the curvature helps determine momentum.


Barrel Toroid Magnet
Huge superconducting coils wrap around the central ATLAS detector.
What it does: The barrel toroid provides a magnetic field for the surrounding muon spectrometer.
Why it matters: It bends muon trajectories so the outer chambers can measure muon momenta independently of the inner tracker.


End-cap Toroid Magnet
Toroid magnets at both ends of ATLAS extend the magnetic field into the forward regions.
What it does: Like the barrel toroid, these magnets bend charged muons rather than directly recording their energy.
Why it matters: They enable momentum measurements for muons that leave the detector closer to the beam direction.


Muon Chambers
Muons can reach detectors far beyond the calorimeters.
What it measures: Muon trajectories in barrel and end-cap chambers, including the New Small Wheel system.
Why it matters: Together with the magnetic field, these measurements help identify muons and determine their momenta.

title: ATLAS Detector
text:
How the Detector Works
The innermost tracking system records the paths of charged particles. A magnetic field bends those trajectories, allowing their momenta to be reconstructed. Calorimeters measure the energy deposited by electrons, photons, and hadrons. Farther out, muon chambers record muons that pass through the inner systems. Together, these measurements help reconstruct the particles produced in a collision.

title: ATLAS Detector
text:
Calorimetry
ATLAS calorimeters measure particle energy by sampling the showers produced as particles pass through alternating absorber and active layers. The system combines a central steel-and-scintillator Tile calorimeter with liquid-argon (LAr) calorimeters covering the electromagnetic, hadronic end-cap, and forward regions.
Select Full Detector to view the official labelled calorimeter cutaway, or choose R–z Layout to examine the longitudinal arrangement near the beam axis.

Full detector calorimeter view

Figure sources: ATLAS Collaboration, Run 3 detector paper, Figure 5 (ATLAS Collaboration 2024b) · ATLAS Experiment © CERN · Official image. R–z schematic adapted from the ATLAS detector paper, Figure 5.19 (ATLAS Collaboration 2008).

Electromagnetic calorimeters (EMB and EMEC). The LAr electromagnetic barrel (EMB) and electromagnetic end-cap (EMEC) measure showers initiated primarily by electrons and photons. Layers of lead absorbers and liquid argon provide fine spatial sampling of deposited energy.
Tile hadronic calorimeters. A central barrel and two extended barrels use steel absorbers and scintillating tiles to sample hadronic showers. These measure much of the energy carried by strongly interacting particles in the central region.
Hadronic end-cap calorimeters (HEC). Located at larger angles to the beam than the FCal, the HEC uses copper absorbers and liquid argon to measure hadronic energy in the end-cap region.
Forward calorimeters (FCal). Close to the beam axis, the FCal extends coverage to approximately 3.1<|η|<4.93.1 < |\eta| < 4.9. Each end-cap contains three LAr modules: FCal1 uses copper absorbers for electromagnetic showers, while FCal2 and FCal3 use tungsten absorbers for hadronic showers. In the R–z view, their order along the beam direction is visible alongside the EMEC and HEC modules.
Here, pseudorapidity η\eta describes direction relative to the beam: larger |η||\eta| corresponds to particles travelling closer to the beam axis.

text:
What Parts of the Detector I Use in My Analysis
My heavy-ion analyses combine charged-particle tracks in the Inner Detector, forward transverse energy in the FCal, and very-forward neutron energy in the Zero Degree Calorimeters (ZDCs). Together, these measurements provide the physics observables, event classification, and pileup rejection used in the analysis.

Measurement used

Inner Detector: Charged-Particle Tracking
The Inner Detector is the main ATLAS system for reconstructing charged particles near midrapidity—the central detector region, away from the beam directions. It provides precision tracking over approximately |η|<2.5|\eta| < 2.5 and surrounds the beam pipe with several nested tracking layers, so particles emerging from the collision leave a sequence of spatial measurements as they move outward through the detector.

Tracking concept



Simplified transverse view of ATLAS tracking.


Conceptual tracking illustration (not to scale). The curved track is fitted using measurements from successive detector layers.


Detector-layer details



Detailed ATLAS tracking detector cutaway and measurement diagrams.


Pixel sensors provide two-dimensional measurements; stereo SCT modules combine strip measurements; TRT straws provide drift-time measurements and transition-radiation information. Detector geometry: ATLAS Collaboration, detector paper, Figure 4.2. This measurement-principle composite is reproduced in X. Ai et al., ACTS for gaseous tracking detectors (FTCF 2024), slide 6. ATLAS Experiment © CERN.


Momentum Measurement


The interactive curvature diagram is an optional enhancement. The complete derivation remains below.



From detector hits to transverse momentum
1. Fit a curved track. Position measurements across the Pixel, SCT, and TRT layers are combined into a trajectory. The track fit determines its curvature using the known magnetic field. The geometry below explains the basic idea with a circular arc.



Sagitta construction for a curved trajectory.


Original explanatory SVG. The three-point sagitta construction illustrates the geometry of curvature; ATLAS fits many detector measurements.
2. Determine the curvature radius. For a circle, the chord length LL and sagitta ss form a right triangle. The Pythagorean theorem gives
R2=(R−s)2+(L2)2,R=L28s+s2.
R^2 = (R-s)^2 + \left(\frac{L}{2}\right)^2,
\qquad
R = \frac{L^2}{8s} + \frac{s}{2}.

For a small sagitta, s≪Ls \ll L, the second term is small, so R≈L2/(8s)R \approx L^2/(8s). Less bending means a smaller sagitta and a larger curvature radius.
3. Convert curvature to momentum. In a uniform magnetic field, the transverse Lorentz force is the force required to bend the transverse momentum:
|q|vTB=pTvTR⇒pT=|q|BR,
|q|v_{\mathrm{T}}B = \frac{p_{\mathrm{T}}v_{\mathrm{T}}}{R}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
p_{\mathrm{T}} = |q|BR,

and in practical high-energy-physics units,
pT[GeV/c]≈0.2998|z|B[T]R[m].
p_{\mathrm{T}}\,[\mathrm{GeV}/c]
\approx 0.2998\,|z|\,B\,[\mathrm{T}]\,R\,[\mathrm{m}].

Here z=q/ez=q/e is the signed charge number. With B≈2TB \approx 2\,\mathrm{T} and the usual singly charged track assumption (|z|=1|z|=1), pT[GeV/c]≈0.6R[m]p_{\mathrm{T}}\,[\mathrm{GeV}/c] \approx 0.6R\,[\mathrm{m}]. The bending direction gives the charge sign; identifying the particle species is not required under this charge assumption.
Educational approximation: the interactive arcs use a uniform 2 T solenoidal field and idealized measurements. Real ATLAS track fits account for magnetic-field variations, measurement uncertainties, material interactions, and multiple scattering. Layer radii follow the ATLAS Inner Detector documentation and published barrel geometry specifications. Field strength: ATLAS Magnet System.






Tracking reconstruction
In broad terms, tracking works in three steps. First, the Pixel detector, the silicon microstrip tracker (SCT), and the transition radiation tracker (TRT) record discrete position measurements, usually called hits. Second, pattern- recognition algorithms identify groups of hits that belong to the same particle and fit them to a common trajectory. Third, because the particle moves in the ATLAS solenoidal magnetic field, the trajectory bends: the amount of curvature determines the transverse momentum pTp_{\mathrm{T}}, while the direction of curvature identifies the sign of the electric charge. The fitted trajectory also gives the particle’s direction and point of closest approach to the collision vertex.
For my analyses, each reconstructed track supplies its transverse momentum pTp_{\mathrm{T}}, pseudorapidity η\eta, and azimuthal angle ϕ\phi. These quantities are used to measure charged-particle multiplicity, event-by-event mean transverse momentum, and flow vectors. The tracking system is therefore the detector element that directly measures the particles entering the core physics observables.



Forward Calorimeters: Event Selection and Centrality
The forward calorimeters measure transverse energy at large pseudorapidity, separated from the midrapidity tracks used in my analysis. Their summed energy ΣET\Sigma E_{\mathrm{T}} defines event-activity or centrality percentiles. The relationship between those percentiles and the overlap geometry of the colliding nuclei is inferred with a Glauber-based collision model rather than measured directly by the FCal.
Using forward energy for event classification and inner-detector tracks for the physics observables helps reduce self-correlations—artificial relationships that can appear when the same particles influence both the event class and the observable. The separation between tracking and forward calorimetry is therefore an important part of the analysis strategy.


Zero Degree Calorimeters: Pileup Rejection
Pileup occurs when more than one Pb+Pb collision is recorded in the same bunch crossing. Signals from those collisions overlap, so the detector can appear to have more activity than was produced by any one collision. This can bias centrality and other event-by-event measurements that assume each recorded event contains a single nuclear collision.
The two Zero Degree Calorimeters are installed about 140 m on either side of the ATLAS interaction point, close to the outgoing beam directions. They measure very-forward neutral particles, primarily spectator neutrons that continue along the beam line after the collision (Avoni et al. 2025).
Each ZDC is a sampling calorimeter. Alternating tungsten absorber plates and fused-silica rods convert the incident neutron’s shower into Cherenkov light, which is directed through a light guide to a photomultiplier tube.
In the Pb+Pb analysis, a genuine single collision follows an expected relationship between the forward-neutron energy recorded in the ZDCs and the FCal ΣET\Sigma E_{\mathrm{T}}. Events with an incompatible combination of ZDC and FCal energy are identified as pileup and removed. The ZDC measurement therefore supports event cleaning rather than entering the final physics observables directly (ATLAS Collaboration 2024a; Avoni et al. 2025).

The upper panel shows the ZDCs housed inside the two TANs (Target Absorbers for Neutrals), 140 m from central ATLAS. Each TAN absorbs the intense flux of very-forward neutral particles and protects downstream LHC magnets. The lower panel defines the ATLAS coordinate system. title: About Me
text:
I am a physicist pursuing a Ph.D. in Nuclear Chemistry at Stony Brook University, working with Prof. Jiangyong Jia. My research explores how nuclear geometry and the dynamics of the quark-gluon plasma are reflected in the particles produced in high-energy nuclear collisions.
I work primarily with the ATLAS Collaboration at CERN and am also a member of the STAR Collaboration at Brookhaven National Laboratory. My research combines experimental data analysis with phenomenological modeling, with particular emphasis on collective flow, event-by-event fluctuations, and nuclear structure.


A central question in my research is how to connect experimentally measured observables to the underlying physics of a nuclear collision. In particular, I am interested in separating the influence of the initial nuclear geometry from the collective response of the evolving medium.
Addressing these questions requires a combination of experimental measurements, analytical calculations, Monte Carlo simulations, and hydrodynamic modeling. This approach connects my work on radial-flow fluctuations in Pb+Pb collisions with studies of nuclear-structure effects in smaller systems such as O+O and Ne+Ne collisions.
I am also interested in understanding which features of an observable provide robust physical information and how different sources of fluctuations can be disentangled.



I completed a five-year Integrated M.Sc. in Physics at the National Institute of Science Education and Research (NISER), Bhubaneswar, India, in 2021, with a minor in Computer Science. I subsequently joined Stony Brook University to pursue my doctoral research in nuclear chemistry.



For research-related inquiries, I can be reached at aman.dimri@stonybrook.edu.

title: Aman Dimri
text:
Research Approach & Future Directions
I aim to find the simple ideas behind complex problems—and turn that understanding into useful solutions. My background in physics and computer science has taught me to bring mathematical reasoning, computational methods, and algorithmic thinking together in that search. Applying these approaches to demanding research questions has sharpened my intuition for recognizing promising directions. That experience has given me the confidence to tackle difficult problems and find a way forward.
Sometimes progress begins with a sudden insight that brings the key idea into focus. Other times, it emerges through patient exploration: questioning assumptions, testing different approaches, and gradually refining an idea until it becomes clear and defensible. Both paths combine creativity with the discipline of testing ideas against evidence. When progress slows, I explore other possibilities and seek fresh perspectives through collaboration.
My research in nuclear physics has given me a strong foundation for pursuing new questions with curiosity and scientific rigor. I am eager to apply this approach to challenging problems across science and technology, from fundamental research to practical applications. I want to pursue these challenges by building on what I know, learning what I need, and exploring possibilities I can’t yet see.

title: Aman Dimri
text:
Research Interests
My current research and emerging interests span five areas—from nuclear physics to artificial intelligence—connected by the challenge of understanding complex behavior and determining which conclusions the evidence truly supports.

Collective Flow & Its Fluctuations: Investigating how transverse momentum correlations and their event-by-event fluctuations reveal the collective dynamics and transport properties of the quark–gluon plasma.
Constraining Nuclear Structure Through High Energy Collisions: Investigating how nuclear structure, particularly nuclear deformation, influences measurable observables in high-energy collisions, and using this sensitivity to constrain the properties of nuclei that are difficult to characterize through conventional methods.
Phenomenology & Modeling: Developing analytical and computational approaches to connect initial-state physics, subsequent hydrodynamic evolution, and the final experimental measurements in high-energy nuclear collisions.
Nuclear Matter & the Equation of State: I am interested in how the nuclear equation of state, relating pressure to density, temperature, and composition, connects atomic nuclei, heavy-ion collisions, and neutron stars. These systems probe complementary regimes of strongly interacting matter.
Artificial Intelligence & Reliable Reasoning: Exploring how AI systems reason with scientific evidence, handle uncertainty and conflicting information, and how their reliability and robustness can be evaluated and improved.

title: Aman Dimri
text:
Featured Research

Evidence for the Collective Nature of Radial Flow



Radial flow characterizes the outward expansion of the quark-gluon plasma produced in heavy-ion collisions. My recent work with the ATLAS Collaboration provided evidence for the collective nature of radial-flow fluctuations through the first measurement of the differential observable \(v_0(p_T)\) in high-energy Pb+Pb collisions at a nucleon-pair center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV.


The observed long-range correlations, transverse-momentum factorization, and centrality-independent response shape provide complementary signatures of a collective origin for radial-flow fluctuations. Comparison with hydrodynamic calculations further revealed a distinctive sensitivity of the measured \(v_0(p_T)\) shape to the bulk viscosity of the quark-gluon plasma.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
Aman Dimri, Somadutta Bhatta, and Jiangyong Jia
Quark Matter 2025
Frankfurt am Main, Germany · April 2025

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
Overview
This poster presented a differential view of radial-flow fluctuations using the observable \(v_0(p_T)\). While earlier work had already established the collective nature of radial flow in Pb+Pb collisions, this poster focused on two specific issues that are essential for interpreting the measurement: the role of non-flow contamination and the impact of multiplicity fluctuations.
The goal was to understand which observed features of the differential observable arise from genuine collective dynamics and which may instead reflect biases from particle production or short-range correlations.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
The Differential Observable
Radial flow is commonly quantified through event-by-event fluctuations of the mean transverse momentum, \([p_T]\). A differential version of this idea probes how fluctuations in the local particle spectrum at a given \(p_T\) are correlated with fluctuations in the event-wise radial-flow signal.
The poster discussed two related formulations of differential radial flow:

\(v_0(p_T)\), based on the normalized spectrum \(n(p_T)\),
\(v_0'(p_T)\), based on the full spectrum \(N(p_T)\).

These two constructions are closely related, but they do not respond in the same way to multiplicity fluctuations. Their difference therefore provides a useful handle on the underlying particle-production dynamics.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
What the Poster Examined
The poster focused on two physics questions.
First, it examined whether characteristic features seen in the measured \(v_0(p_T)\) could be influenced by non-flow effects, especially at high \(p_T\). For this purpose, HIJING was used as a non-collective baseline model.
Second, it studied how global multiplicity fluctuations modify the differential observable, and how the comparison between \(v_0(p_T)\) and \(v_0'(p_T)\) can be used to isolate that contribution.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
Impact of Non-Flow Bias
A central point of the poster was that the behavior of \(v_0(p_T)\) in HIJING differs qualitatively from the collective expectation.
In particular:

the factorization behavior is broken in HIJING,
the result depends on the choice of the reference \(p_T\) range,
and \(v_0(p_T)\) rises approximately linearly at high \(p_T\).

These observations support the interpretation that some of the splitting behavior and the strong rise at large \(p_T\) seen in peripheral data are likely influenced by non-flow contamination rather than pure collective radial flow.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
Impact of Multiplicity Fluctuations
The second major message was that \(v_0(p_T)\) itself is comparatively stable across different event ensembles, while \(v_0'(p_T)\) is more sensitive to multiplicity fluctuations.
This makes the difference
\[
v_0'(p_T) - v_0(p_T)
\]
a useful diagnostic quantity. The poster showed that this difference is approximately constant in \(p_T\), consistent with the expectation that it isolates the contribution from multiplicity fluctuations.
This provides a new way to constrain fluctuations in the particle-production process, especially when varying the event classifier or rapidity interval.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
Main Takeaways
The poster highlighted two main conclusions:

some features of the measured differential radial-flow signal, especially the splitting behavior and the large-\(p_T\) rise in peripheral events, can be attributed to non-flow contamination;
the difference between the two formulations of differential radial flow can be used to isolate and understand multiplicity fluctuations.

Together, these results sharpen the interpretation of \(v_0(p_T)\) and clarify how this observable can be used as a robust probe of collective dynamics.

title: Is Differential Radial Flow Collective?
text:
Relation to the Publication
This poster should be viewed as a companion presentation to the project
“The shape of differential radial flow \(v_0(p_T)\), not its zero-crossing, carries physical information”
Nuclear Science and Techniques 37, 163 (2026).
While the publication develops the main physical interpretation of the differential radial-flow observable, this poster emphasized two additional practical aspects: how to identify non-flow contributions and how to use the difference between alternative definitions to probe multiplicity fluctuations.

title: Building and Characterizing a Diode-Pumped Nd:YAG Laser
text:
Overview
A working laser depends on more than choosing a gain medium. The optical pump, resonator geometry, and alignment must work together to establish and sustain lasing. In this Integrated Master’s laboratory project, I assembled and aligned a diode-pumped neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG) laser from a modular optical setup, then investigated its output characteristics and several features of its dynamics.
The experiments began with the 808 nm pump diode and the generation of 1064 nm infrared laser light. I then measured lasing thresholds and output power, examined transient spiking, and used a potassium titanyl phosphate (KTP) crystal to generate green light at 532 nm through second-harmonic generation. Finally, I studied the transverse intensity patterns of the frequency-doubled beam. The work combined patient optical alignment with quantitative measurements and numerical analysis of the results.

title: Building and Characterizing a Diode-Pumped Nd:YAG Laser
text:
Experimental Setup
The system used a temperature-controlled diode laser to optically pump a Nd:YAG crystal. Collimating and focusing optics directed the pump light into the gain medium, which formed part of an adjustable resonator. The output was characterized using an optical power meter, a photodiode detector, and an oscilloscope. For frequency doubling, a KTP crystal was introduced into the resonator to convert part of the 1064 nm radiation into 532 nm light.






Figure 1: Optical arrangement of the diode-pumped Nd:YAG laser. Original schematic adapted from LD DIDACTIC/LEYBOLD, Diode Pumped Nd:YAG Laser, manual 4747106 EN; component labels updated for clarity.









Figure 2: Original photograph of the optical-bench arrangement used for second-harmonic diffraction measurements (Figure 20 of the laboratory report).



A major practical challenge was achieving a common optical axis through the pump optics, Nd:YAG crystal, and resonator mirrors. The alignment was refined iteratively until stable laser operation could be obtained.

title: Building and Characterizing a Diode-Pumped Nd:YAG Laser
text:
Methods

Aligning and characterizing the laser
We first characterized the pump diode by varying its injection current and temperature. Absorption measurements through the Nd:YAG crystal helped locate a favorable pump-wavelength region; the report discusses an absorption feature consistent with pumping near 808.4 nm, while noting that the limited temperature range did not establish an unambiguous spectral assignment.
After aligning the resonator, we measured the infrared output power as a function of pump-diode current. These measurements were used to identify the onset of lasing and its approximately linear operating region. Output-power measurements at different diode temperatures also illustrated the sensitivity of the laser to pump wavelength and optical alignment.


Measuring the excited-state lifetime and transient response
We monitored the photodetector signal after changing the pumping conditions. Assuming an exponential decay,
\[
V(t) = V_0 e^{-t/\tau},
\]
we estimated the lifetime of the Nd:YAG \(^4F_{3/2}\) metastable level using the time at which the measured signal fell to \(V_0/e\). Ten repetitions were used to estimate its mean and spread. The report notes a photodetector response time of approximately \(10\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) for the selected gain setting.
In pulsed operation, we also recorded the time between turning on the pump and the first large laser-output spike. The relationship between this delay and pump current was investigated using empirical fits.


Frequency doubling and beam profiles
To explore nonlinear optical behavior, we inserted a KTP frequency-doubling crystal inside the resonator. We observed green second-harmonic light at 532 nm and measured how its external output power changed with the measured fundamental output. Finally, we recorded the shapes of several transverse laser modes and compared their intensity distributions with expected beam profiles.

title: Building and Characterizing a Diode-Pumped Nd:YAG Laser
text:
Results and Interpretation

Lasing thresholds and excited-state lifetime
The two stages of the optical system showed distinct output-power responses to pump-diode current. The measured thresholds and the excited-state lifetime are summarized below.







Measurement
Reported result




Pump-diode lasing threshold
\(144.004 \pm 1.756\ \mathrm{mA}\)


Nd:YAG lasing onset, expressed as pump-diode current
\(140.426 \pm 4.218\ \mathrm{mA}\)


Nd:YAG \(^4F_{3/2}\) lifetime
\(263.5\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) (sample standard deviation: \(10.5\ \mu\mathrm{s}\))



The lifetime was estimated from ten oscilloscope measurements. The stated \(10.5\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) characterizes the spread of those measurements, rather than a complete uncertainty budget; the detector response time was assessed separately in the report. The Nd:YAG output became approximately linear over an intermediate current range and showed signs of saturation at higher pump currents.






Figure 3: Optical output as a function of pump-diode injection current. Left: the pump diode; right: Nd:YAG output at 1064 nm. Points reproduce the measurements from the report’s Tables 12.3 and 12.4. Dashed markers indicate threshold currents quoted in the report, rather than thresholds determined by a new fit.





Pump-temperature sensitivity
The Nd:YAG output also depended on the diode temperature, which changes the pump wavelength and its overlap with the crystal absorption spectrum. The measured dependence varied with the fixed injection current, as illustrated below. The lines connect measured points and do not represent an additional fit or a temperature-to-wavelength calibration.






Figure 4: Nd:YAG output as a function of pump-diode temperature for injection currents of 320, 470, and 600 mA. Curves join the measured observations from Table 12.5; they are not fitted models.





Transient spiking
When the pump was switched on, the laser output did not immediately settle to its steady-state value. Instead, a large initial spike appeared after a measurable delay. The report found that, over the measured current range, the delay was approximately described by
\[
t_{\mathrm{delay}} \propto (I-I_{\mathrm{th}})^{-1/3},
\]
where \(I\) is the pump-diode injection current and \(I_{\mathrm{th}}\) is a threshold determined by the empirical fit. This behavior illustrated the transient response of the coupled population inversion and intracavity light field.






Figure 5: Delay before the first laser-output spike as a function of pump-diode injection current, using all 34 observations from Table 12.7. New unweighted fits compare a free exponent with a fixed exponent of \(-1/3\).



For these reconstructed plots, a new unweighted fit gives an empirical exponent of approximately \(-0.361\) and an onset parameter \(I_0\approx145.8\ \mathrm{mA}\). These are fit results from the tabulated spiking data, distinct from the lasing thresholds reported above. The \(-1/3\) behavior remains a useful approximation over the measured current range, rather than an exact relation.


Second-harmonic generation
With the KTP crystal inside the resonator, the infrared output at 1064 nm produced visible green light at 532 nm. In this setup, the green signal was not observed when the crystal was placed outside the resonator, consistent with the importance of the higher intracavity intensity for this nonlinear process. The measured output powers followed an approximately quadratic relationship,
\[
P_{2\omega} \propto P_{\omega}^{2},
\]
as expected in the regime considered in the report. Because the fundamental and second-harmonic powers were measured at different outputs of the optical system, their numerical ratio should not be treated directly as a conversion efficiency.






Figure 6: Externally measured power at 532 nm versus externally measured power at 1064 nm from Table 12.6, with a new unweighted fit to \(P_{532}=a(P_{1064}-b)^2\). The output-power ratio is not a measurement of intracavity conversion efficiency.



The fitted quadratic describes the tabulated external powers. Its parameters were newly estimated from the original table; they should not be interpreted as an independently calibrated optical conversion efficiency or an observed zero-power offset.


Transverse laser modes
The frequency-doubled output also exhibited distinct transverse intensity patterns. The fundamental \(\mathrm{TEM}_{00}\) mode appeared as a single bright spot, with an approximately Gaussian transverse profile. Higher-order modes showed multiple lobes and nodes; the \(\mathrm{TEM}_{10}\) pattern provides a clear two-lobed example.






Figure 7: Illustrative transverse laser modes of the frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser. Each pair shows a representative beam pattern (left) and an idealized three-dimensional intensity surface (right): (a,b) \(\mathrm{TEM}_{00}\); (c,d) \(\mathrm{TEM}_{10}\); (e,f) \(\mathrm{TEM}_{20}\); (g,h) \(\mathrm{TEM}_{02}\); (i,j) \(\mathrm{TEM}_{30}\); (k,l) \(\mathrm{TEM}_{22}\). The images are illustrative, enhanced for clarity, and are not the original measured intensity profiles. Experimental photographs and profiles appear in the laboratory report.

title: Building and Characterizing a Diode-Pumped Nd:YAG Laser
text:
Conclusions
The project connected the construction and alignment of an optical instrument with measurements of the physics it makes accessible. We established Nd:YAG laser operation, measured its power characteristics and metastable-state lifetime, observed transient spiking, generated a visible second harmonic, and investigated transverse beam modes. It was a practical introduction to how sensitive experimental systems are assembled, calibrated, and understood through careful measurement and analysis.

title: Effect of Nuclear Shape Parameters On Initial State Observables In Heavy Ion Collisions
text:
Summary
The initial geometry of a heavy-ion collision is influenced by several properties of the colliding nuclei, including quadrupole deformation, triaxiality, nuclear radius, and skin depth. This poster examined how variations and fluctuations of these nuclear-shape parameters modify observables related to elliptic and radial flow.
The study focused on the initial-state eccentricity and inverse transverse size, investigating their dependence on nuclear deformation across different collision systems. The results showed that fluctuations of the quadrupole deformation enhance the fluctuations of these observables, while triaxiality fluctuations reduce the differences between prolate and oblate nuclear configurations.
