title: Probing Effect of Nuclear Shape Coexistence in Heavy-Ion Collisions using Glauber Model
text:
Summary
Nuclear deformation can influence both the initial geometry and final-state observables in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. This presentation explored an additional aspect of nuclear structure: shape coexistence, in which a nucleus can exhibit multiple competing geometric configurations.
Using a Glauber-model description of the collision geometry, the study investigated how shape coexistence modifies initial-state observables relevant for heavy-ion collisions, including eccentricity and transverse-area fluctuations. The work provided an early step toward connecting nuclear-structure information from low-energy measurements with observables accessible in relativistic nuclear collisions.

title: Revealing Nuclear Geometry with O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions
text:
ATLAS Collaboration
Physical Review C 113, 045205 (2026)

title: Revealing Nuclear Geometry with O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions
text:
Overview
The shape of a colliding nucleus influences the geometry of the matter created in a high-energy nuclear collision. As this matter expands, its initial spatial anisotropy is converted into an anisotropy in the directions of the produced particles. Collective flow can therefore reveal properties of the incoming nuclei, connecting measurements of the quark–gluon plasma (QGP) with questions traditionally addressed by nuclear-structure physics.
This project studies that connection using the first ATLAS measurements of azimuthal flow in \(^{16}\)O+\(^{16}\)O and \(^{20}\)Ne+\(^{20}\)Ne collisions at \(\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=5.36\) TeV, recorded at the LHC in 2025. Oxygen and neon are similar in size but have different predicted intrinsic shapes, making their comparison particularly sensitive to nuclear geometry. The central result is an enhancement of elliptic flow, \(v_2\), in Ne+Ne relative to O+O collisions, consistent with the pronounced prolate deformation of the neon nucleus. The four-particle cumulant measurements provide especially strong sensitivity to this difference.

title: Revealing Nuclear Geometry with O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions
text:
Analysis

Why compare oxygen and neon?
In non-central nuclear collisions, the offset between the two colliding nuclei produces an almond-shaped overlap region. In the most central collisions, this impact-parameter contribution becomes small, and fluctuations and the intrinsic shapes of the nuclei play a larger role. Light-ion collisions are consequently a useful setting in which to study the influence of nuclear structure on collective motion.
Nuclear-structure calculations describe \(^{16}\)O as approximately spherical, with possible tetrahedral \(\alpha\)-cluster correlations, whereas \(^{20}\)Ne is predicted to have a pronounced prolate, or elongated, configuration. The latter is often described as a bowling-pin-like shape. Because the two nuclei have comparable masses, taking ratios of their flow measurements reduces several shared size-dependent and experimental effects, making the differences more sensitive to the initial nuclear geometry.






Figure 1: Illustration of the contrasting nuclear shapes and the ordering of measured elliptic flow in central Ne+Ne, O+O, and Pb+Pb collisions. The nuclear density profiles are schematic; the corresponding experimental comparison is discussed in the ATLAS Physics Briefing.





From initial geometry to anisotropic flow
The final-state azimuthal distribution is characterized by the flow coefficients \(v_n\), which quantify the Fourier harmonics of particle emission. In a simple hydrodynamic response picture, the elliptic and triangular harmonics are related to the corresponding initial-state eccentricities through
\[
v_n \simeq \kappa_n\varepsilon_n, \qquad n=2,3,
\]
where \(\varepsilon_n\) describes the initial spatial anisotropy and \(\kappa_n\) encodes the collective response. This relation is approximate, but it illustrates the basic principle: differences in the intrinsic geometry of oxygen and neon can survive the expansion and appear as differences in the measured \(v_n\). Elliptic flow, \(v_2\), is especially sensitive to an elongated initial configuration, while triangular flow, \(v_3\), provides complementary information about event-by-event geometry fluctuations.


Measuring flow and its fluctuations
ATLAS measured the flow harmonics \(v_2\), \(v_3\), and \(v_4\) as functions of transverse momentum, charged-particle multiplicity, and collision centrality. The analysis combines two complementary methods. Two-particle azimuthal correlations, with a template-fit subtraction, measure the flow harmonics while reducing the contributions of jets and other non-flow correlations. Four-particle subevent cumulants use higher-order particle correlations to suppress non-flow and probe different moments of the event-by-event flow distribution.
The four-particle cumulant is defined by
\[
c_n\{4\}=\langle\!\langle\{4\}_n\rangle\!\rangle
-2\langle\!\langle\{2\}_n\rangle\!\rangle^2,
\qquad v_n\{4\}=\bigl(-c_n\{4\}\bigr)^{1/4},
\]
where \(\{2\}_n\) and \(\{4\}_n\) are the two- and four-particle azimuthal correlations and the double brackets denote ensemble averages; \(v_n\{4\}\) is defined when \(c_n\{4\}<0\). Unlike the two-particle measurement, which is sensitive to the mean squared flow magnitude, the four-particle measurement also constrains the structure of its event-by-event fluctuations. Comparing \(v_n\{2\}\) and \(v_n\{4\}\) thus provides additional information about the initial nuclear geometry.


Experimental signatures of collectivity
Both O+O and Ne+Ne collisions exhibit the hierarchy \(v_2>v_3>v_4\). The measured \(v_2(p_{\mathrm{T}})\) rises at low transverse momentum and decreases after a maximum around \(2\)–\(4\) GeV, following trends familiar from larger heavy-ion systems. These features are consistent with a collective response in the light-ion systems, although their detailed interpretation requires control of non-flow contributions and initial-state fluctuations.
The difference between the two- and four-particle measurements becomes more pronounced toward high multiplicity, revealing the increasing relative role of flow fluctuations in central events. This motivates examining not only the magnitudes of the individual harmonics but also their ratios between the two collision systems.


The nuclear-shape signal in central collisions
The most direct signature comes from the Ne+Ne/O+O ratios of the flow harmonics. For centralities more peripheral than approximately 10%, the \(v_2\) ratios vary relatively little with centrality. Toward the most central collisions, however, both the two- and four-particle elliptic-flow ratios increase. The enhancement is more pronounced for \(v_2\{4\}\), making the four-particle cumulant comparison particularly sensitive to the difference in intrinsic nuclear shape.
The triangular-flow measurements provide a useful contrast. The two-particle \(v_3\) ratio decreases toward the most central collisions, becoming comparable between Ne+Ne and O+O in the 0–1% interval. Together, these observations favor an interpretation in which neon’s elongated geometry contributes to the enhanced elliptic response, rather than a uniform increase of all flow harmonics. The multiplicity-dependent and centrality-dependent comparisons are presented in Fig. 6 and Fig. 7 of the ATLAS paper, respectively.


Comparison with nuclear-structure models
The measurements are also compared with hydrodynamic calculations incorporating microscopic nuclear configurations. Models using nuclear structures from the projected generator coordinate method, together with different descriptions of initial energy deposition, reproduce some aspects of the O+O and Ne+Ne systematics but differ in their ability to describe the centrality dependence. In particular, the observed central enhancement of the \(v_2\) ratio is described more successfully by the calculation combining nuclear-structure inputs with Trento initial conditions than by the calculation using IP-Glasma initial conditions.
This comparison illustrates both the value and the challenge of using flow as a nuclear-structure probe. The data are sensitive to the intrinsic shapes of the nuclei, but extracting quantitative nuclear-structure constraints also requires control of the initial-state model and the subsequent hydrodynamic response.

title: Revealing Nuclear Geometry with O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions
text:
My Contribution
As a member of the ATLAS primary analysis group, I served as the main analyst for the multi-particle cumulant measurements in O+O and Ne+Ne collisions. This work supplied the four-particle flow observables that probe event-by-event fluctuations and give the strongest sensitivity to the nuclear-shape difference in the elliptic-flow comparison. I also presented the first ATLAS O+O and Ne+Ne flow results in a plenary talk at Initial Stages 2025.

title: Revealing Nuclear Geometry with O+O and Ne+Ne Collisions
text:
Broader Implications
The O+O and Ne+Ne measurements demonstrate how relativistic collisions of light nuclei can connect two complementary questions: what shapes do nuclei have, and how does the matter they create respond collectively to those shapes? Comparing systems with similar size but different intrinsic geometry provides constraints on nuclear-structure calculations while testing hydrodynamic and initial-state models in small collision systems.
The pronounced sensitivity of \(v_2\{4\}\) also establishes higher-order flow correlations as an important part of this program. More precise measurements, together with improved model calculations, may help distinguish the effects of nuclear deformation, clustering, and event-by-event initial-state fluctuations.

title: Evidence for the Collective Nature of Radial Flow
text:
ATLAS Collaboration
Physical Review Letters 136, 032301 (2026)

title: Evidence for the Collective Nature of Radial Flow
text:
Overview
Radial flow is one of the fundamental manifestations of the collective expansion of the quark–gluon plasma (QGP). While anisotropic flow has been extensively established as a collective phenomenon and developed into a precision probe of QGP properties, comparable direct experimental evidence for the global collective nature of radial flow had been missing. This work introduces the first measurement of the transverse-momentum dependence of radial-flow fluctuations, \(v_0(p_T)\), over \(0.5 < p_T < 10\) GeV in Pb+Pb collisions at \(\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=5.02\) TeV with the ATLAS detector. The measurement tests radial flow against three characteristic hallmarks of collectivity: long-range correlations in pseudorapidity, factorization in \(p_T\), and a centrality-independent response shape. All three are observed in the flow-dominated regime, providing direct experimental evidence for the global collective nature of radial flow. Beyond establishing collectivity, comparisons with hydrodynamic calculations demonstrate that \(v_0(p_T)\) is sensitive to the bulk viscosity of the QGP. The measurement therefore establishes differential radial flow as a new tool for studying both the collective dynamics and transport properties of the strongly interacting QGP medium.

title: Evidence for the Collective Nature of Radial Flow
text:
Analysis

Why establish radial-flow collectivity?
The collective expansion of the quark–gluon plasma can manifest itself through two complementary forms of flow. Anisotropic flow reflects the hydrodynamic response to the initial spatial shape of the collision, while radial flow reflects the response to fluctuations in the transverse size and density of the system.
For anisotropic flow, its collective origin has been established experimentally through a broad set of characteristic signatures, including long-range correlations, factorization, and a universal hydrodynamic response. Radial flow, despite being of comparable fundamental importance, had not been subjected to the same direct experimental tests.
This distinction matters because radial-flow observables are increasingly being used to constrain properties of the QGP. Event-by-event fluctuations of the mean transverse momentum, \([p_T]\), exhibit striking behavior in ultra-central Pb+Pb collisions, including a sharp suppression of their variance and a rapid increase of \(\langle[p_T]\rangle\) with multiplicity. These features have been interpreted within a hydrodynamic picture in which radial-flow fluctuations originate from both global collision geometry and local density fluctuations.
Before such observables can be used as precision probes of the QGP equation of state or transport properties, however, an important logical step must be established experimentally: is radial flow itself genuinely collective?


Differential radial flow
To answer this question, the analysis introduces the differential radial-flow observable \(v_0(p_T)\).
Its physical origin can be understood by considering events with approximately fixed total entropy. An event with a smaller transverse collision area develops stronger pressure gradients and therefore experiences a larger radial push. Its particle spectrum becomes flatter and its event-by-event mean transverse momentum \([p_T]\) increases. Conversely, an event with a larger transverse area experiences weaker radial expansion and develops a steeper spectrum.
This produces a characteristic correlation between fluctuations of the local particle yield and fluctuations of \([p_T]\). At low \(p_T\), the two quantities are anticorrelated; near the ensemble mean transverse momentum the correlation crosses zero; and at higher \(p_T\) it becomes positive.
The differential observable is constructed from this correlation,
\[
v_0(p_T)
=
\frac{1}{v_0}
\frac{
\langle \delta n(p_T)\delta[p_T]\rangle
}{
\langle n(p_T)\rangle\langle[p_T]\rangle
},
\]
where \(n(p_T)\) is the normalized particle spectrum and \(v_0\) is the corresponding integrated radial-flow fluctuation.






Figure 1: Schematic illustration of the physical origin of differential radial flow. Events with larger \([p_T]\) have flatter spectra, while events with smaller \([p_T]\) have steeper spectra, producing a characteristic sign change in the correlation between \(\delta n(p_T)\) and \(\delta[p_T]\).



A two-subevent method is used in which the local spectrum and \([p_T]\) are measured using particles separated in pseudorapidity. This suppresses short-range correlations and allows the global component of the radial-flow signal to be isolated.


Experimental hallmarks of collectivity
The key idea of the measurement is to test radial flow against the same experimental criteria that are traditionally used to establish anisotropic collectivity.

Long-range correlations
A global collective expansion should generate correlations extending over large separations in pseudorapidity. Experimentally, \(v_0(p_T)\) is found to be largely insensitive to the pseudorapidity gap used between the two subevents, as shown in Figure 2.






Figure 2: Differential radial flow \(v_0(p_T)\) measured for different pseudorapidity gaps in central and peripheral Pb+Pb collisions. The weak dependence on the gap size demonstrates the long-range nature of the radial-flow correlation.



This behavior is observed in both central and peripheral Pb+Pb collisions. Deviations appear primarily at larger \(p_T\), where contributions from jets and other non-flow effects become increasingly important.


Centrality-independent response
The absolute magnitude of \(v_0(p_T)\) varies strongly with collision centrality. Much of this variation reflects changes in the magnitude of the initial-state size fluctuations rather than changes in the subsequent hydrodynamic response.
To reduce this dependence, the differential measurement is divided by its integrated counterpart, \(v_0\). As shown in Figure 3, the resulting quantity, \(v_0(p_T)/v_0\), exhibits a striking behavior: curves from widely separated centrality intervals collapse onto an approximately common shape in the flow-dominated region.






Figure 3: Differential radial flow \(v_0(p_T)\) for different centrality intervals before and after normalization by the integrated radial-flow fluctuation \(v_0\). The strong centrality dependence of the absolute magnitude is substantially reduced after normalization, revealing an approximately universal response shape in the flow-dominated region.



This centrality-independent shape indicates that very different initial collision geometries are being transformed into momentum space through a common underlying hydrodynamic response.


Factorization
A collective mode generated by a global hydrodynamic expansion is also expected to satisfy factorization. This is tested by changing the reference \(p_T\) interval used to define \([p_T]\) and its event-by-event fluctuations. For \(p_T \lesssim 3\) GeV, the measured \(v_0(p_T)\) is essentially insensitive to this choice, demonstrating factorization in the region dominated by soft collective physics, as shown in Figure 4.






Figure 4: Differential radial flow \(v_0(p_T)\) measured using different reference \(p_T\) ranges in central and peripheral Pb+Pb collisions. The agreement of the measurements at low \(p_T\) demonstrates factorization in the flow-dominated regime.



At larger transverse momentum, the factorization begins to break. In peripheral collisions, this behavior is consistent with increasing contamination from residual non-flow correlations, while in central collisions the high-\(p_T\) response becomes sensitive to jet-quenching phenomena.



Connection to QGP transport properties
Once the collective nature of radial flow is established, the differential observable can be used to investigate properties of the medium itself.
The measured \(v_0(p_T)/v_0\) is compared with hydrodynamic calculations based on the Trento+MUSIC framework. The ideal-hydrodynamic calculation and the calculation including shear viscosity give very similar predictions and underestimate the data at high \(p_T\), failing to reproduce the measured shape. In contrast, the inclusion of a temperature-dependent bulk viscosity, \(\zeta/s(T)\), substantially modifies the high-\(p_T\) behavior and provides a much better description of the data. After additionally accounting for the difference in the mean transverse momentum between model and data by scaling the horizontal axis with \(\bar{p}_T\), the agreement improves further, as shown in Figure 5.






Figure 5: Comparison of the measured scaled differential radial flow with Trento+MUSIC hydrodynamic calculations. The ideal and shear-only calculations underestimate the data at high \(p_T\), while including a temperature-dependent bulk viscosity significantly improves the description. Scaling the horizontal axis by the mean transverse momentum further improves the agreement.



The normalization by the integrated \(v_0\) suppresses much of the influence of the initial-state fluctuation magnitude and emphasizes the hydrodynamic response. The improved description of the measured shape after including bulk viscosity demonstrates the sensitivity of differential radial flow to \(\zeta/s\), establishing \(v_0(p_T)\) as a new experimental probe of QGP transport properties.


Broader implications
By exhibiting long-range correlations, a centrality-independent response shape, and factorization, radial flow satisfies the same key hallmarks of collectivity established for azimuthal flow. These results elevate radial flow to the rigorous standing of azimuthal flow, establishing it as a powerful new probe for constraining QGP transport properties.
The same observable also opens a path toward future system-size studies. Measurements of \(v_0(p_T)\) in systems such as p+O, O+O, Ne+Ne, and other small (p+p) or exotic collision systems (\(\gamma\)+Pb) could provide an independent probe of collectivity, help explore how the emergence of QGP-like behavior evolves with system size, and ultimately help identify the smallest collision systems capable of forming a QGP droplet.

title: Building and Testing a Plastic Scintillation Detector
text:
Overview
A particle detector begins with a physical interaction, but the information we measure is usually an electrical signal. In this project, I worked with my lab partner to build a plastic scintillation detector and use it to measure the mean lifetime of stopped cosmic muons. The aim was to follow the full experimental process: assembling the detector, establishing that it produced usable signals, and testing its performance through a quantitative physics measurement.
We constructed a detector based on an EJ-200 plastic scintillator coupled to a photomultiplier tube (PMT). After verifying its response with an oscilloscope, we connected it to timing and acquisition electronics, recorded candidate stopped-muon decay events, and extracted decay lifetimes from exponential fits using ROOT. We also collected data with an existing laboratory detector for comparison.
This was a collaborative fourth-year Integrated Master’s laboratory project at NISER, carried out with Divyanshu Gupta. The work combined detector assembly, optical coupling, electronic signal processing, calibration, and data analysis.

title: Building and Testing a Plastic Scintillation Detector
text:
Experimental Setup

Turning particle interactions into signals
When an ionizing particle deposits energy in the plastic scintillator, the material emits a short flash of visible light. The EJ-200 scintillator used in our detector emits primarily in the blue region, with a reported emission peak near 425 nm. Photons reaching the PMT release photoelectrons at its photocathode. A dynode chain amplifies the resulting signal into a voltage pulse that can be recorded by electronic instruments.
Efficient light collection depends on the construction of the detector as much as on the choice of scintillating material. Our assembly used several components with distinct roles:

EJ-200 plastic scintillator: Produced the light signals when particles deposited energy in the detector.
EJ-510 reflective coating: Helped redirect scintillation light within the scintillator toward the photosensor.
Black vinyl wrapping: Reduced the entry of ambient light into the assembly.
EJ-560 silicone optical interface: Coupled the scintillator optically to the PMT.
ET-9266B photomultiplier tube: Converted the collected light into measurable electrical pulses.



Building the detector
We cleaned and prepared the scintillator, applied successive reflective coatings, and wrapped the coated surfaces to make the assembly light-tight. We then prepared an acrylic mounting support, coupled the PMT to the scintillator through the optical interface, and secured the completed assembly. Finally, we checked the detector output on an oscilloscope before proceeding to the lifetime measurement.






Figure 1: Construction and testing of the scintillation detector: (a) Preparing the bare scintillator crystal → (b) applying EJ-510 reflective coating → (c) wrapping with black vinyl tape → (d) photomultiplier tube interior → (e) mounting the PMT onto the scintillator → (f) coating the remaining surface → (g) completing the light-tight wrapping → (h) verifying the detector response with an oscilloscope. Photographs from the original laboratory report. Panels (a) and (g) show Divyanshu Gupta; panel (e) shows Dr. Varchaswi K. S. Kashyap.

title: Building and Testing a Plastic Scintillation Detector
text:
Methods

Initial detector tests
To verify that the completed detector responded to particle interactions, we connected the PMT output to a digital oscilloscope and inspected the resulting voltage pulses. The recorded signals established that the assembled scintillator and PMT were functioning together and motivated the next step: measuring a physical quantity using the new detector.


Measuring the lifetime of stopped cosmic muons
A cosmic-ray muon that stops in the scintillator can produce an initial, or prompt, pulse as it loses energy. Its subsequent decay produces a charged particle that can generate a second, delayed, pulse. The interval between these signals provides an estimate of the muon’s decay time. Collecting many such intervals yields a decay-time distribution.
The timing system used a leading-edge discriminator, a time-to-amplitude converter (TAC), and a multichannel analyzer (MCA). The discriminator selected pulses above a chosen threshold. The TAC converted the time interval between selected signals into a pulse amplitude, and the MCA accumulated the corresponding distribution. A pulse generator was used for the time calibration of the MCA.
The discriminator threshold required particular attention. The previously available detector and our newly built detector showed different noise responses at the same threshold. We adjusted the settings and light shielding before collecting the lifetime data. We analyzed the resulting distributions in ROOT using an exponential decay model,
\[
N(\Delta t) = A e^{-\Delta t/\tau_\mu},
\]
where \(\Delta t\) is the recorded time interval and \(\tau_\mu\) is the fitted mean muon lifetime. This is the signal model used for the fits in the report; background contributions were considered during setup and threshold selection.

The constructed detector produced decay-time distributions consistent with the expected exponential behavior. Two data sets were collected with the new detector, giving the following fitted lifetimes:

These uncertainties are the fit uncertainties quoted in the laboratory report. Both results are consistent, within their stated uncertainties, with the reference muon lifetime of approximately \(2.197\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). Measurements with the existing laboratory detector also gave compatible lifetimes, providing a useful comparison for the new assembly.
An important practical result was that the optimal discriminator threshold differed between detectors. The report identifies approximately 10 mV for the original laboratory setup and 15 mV for our constructed detector. Lower thresholds admitted additional noise or background counts, which complicated the observed decay distribution. This showed why reliable measurements require not only a working detector but also careful electronic configuration and calibration.
The reconstructed decay-time spectra below summarize the two threshold settings used for the detector that we built. The 15 mV setting gave the more precise result and was identified in the report as the preferred operating point for our assembled detector, while the 13 mV setting provides a useful comparison.













Figure 2: Stopped cosmic-muon decay-time spectra for the constructed detector. Left: 15 mV discriminator threshold, \(\tau_\mu = 2.230 \pm 0.043\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). Right: 13 mV threshold, \(\tau_\mu = 2.106 \pm 0.092\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).



These figures reconstruct the laboratory report’s rebinned spectra. Error bars illustrate Poisson counting uncertainties inferred from the reconstructed heights, while the curves and lifetime values reproduce the report’s exponential fits. The original MCA count files and the complete calibration record were unavailable, so these plots should be read as faithful reconstructions of the report figures rather than a new raw-data analysis.

title: Building and Testing a Plastic Scintillation Detector
text:
Conclusions
This project demonstrated the complete path from detector construction to a physics measurement. We assembled a plastic scintillator-PMT detector, verified its response, configured the acquisition electronics, and used its signals to measure the lifetime of stopped cosmic muons. The measured lifetimes were consistent with the expected value and with results from the existing laboratory setup.
For me, the most valuable part of the experience was connecting the physical design of a detector to the quality of its measurements. Optical coupling, light shielding, electronic thresholds, calibration, and statistical fitting all influenced the final result.
